_why: John, 12 Oct 2026: on a few passages, readers (Jewish and Christian, or within each) divide over meaning, and tN gives one side or none. These are the one place Yada needs human writing: John or a trusted reviewer writes a fair note giving two or three readings. Until an entry has a note with status 'approved', the reader sees nothing extra and the report flags the passage. In every listed passage, no summary sentence comes from the disputed verses. 'question' is the candidate's subject, for John's list only; it is never shown. Option 3 (John, 12 Oct): instead of prose, John fills 'positions' with two or three readings, each at most 18 words, optionally naming who holds it ('held_by', e.g. 'many Jewish readers'). The app sets them in the Readers differ sentence. Set 'status' to 'approved' when done. Where tN already gives readings, those show meanwhile (option 1). 'kind' (John, 12 Oct): 'data' shows only the JPS 1917 verse (Old Testament) or the manuscript fact; 'tn-readings' shows tN's readings (verse notes, or a chapter introduction that sets out two readings) meanwhile; 'positions' shows nothing until John approves positions; 'held' shows nothing. Each position may carry 'source' (e.g. 'Tyndale Open Study Notes, JHN 6:53-58'), credited under Sources. Positions (John, 12 Oct, supersedes 'note' and the 18-word form): each position is a source's own sentence, unchanged, with 'source' (e.g. 'Tyndale Open Study Notes') and its own 'status'; John approves or rejects each and writes nothing. 'held_by' only where the source's own words say it. Two or more approved positions show; a passage with no source stating two views moves to kind 'held'. 'relation' (John, 12 Oct): 'differ' by default; 'together' where the readings can sit side by side rather than oppose (PSA 2:7, ISA 14:12–15). It changes only Yada's fixed lead-in ('Readers explain this in more than one way'); the slot is still Readers differ and the quotes are never edited.

entries.question: Whether the book is a love poem, an allegory of God and his people, or both

positions.text: Likewise, the Aramaic Targum (interpretive paraphrase) of the Song presents it as the story of God’s relationship with Israel from the Exodus to the future reign of the Messiah.
This allegorical view represents the predominant Jewish and Christian interpretation of the Song from Aqiba’s time through the mid-1800s.

Early Christian interpreters, such as Origen (AD 185–253) and Jerome (AD 347–420), adopted the allegorical interpretation but identified the man as Jesus Christ and the woman as the individual Christian or the church as a whole.

Today it is generally agreed that the Song speaks God’s wisdom into this important area of our lives as human beings: It affirms and celebrates God’s good gift of love and sexuality in the context of marriage.

Many Christians also think that, even though the main meaning of this poem is to give a beautiful portrayal of romantic love between a man and a woman, this book also contains lessons about God’s love for his bride, the Church.

Paul does not speak against good deeds themselves, but about trying to receive forgiveness of sins through good deeds (Rom 3:28; Gal 2:16).
Both Paul and James believed that a person must respond to God's offer of salvation by faith. But they differed in their emphasis.
But, if the Apostle of the Gentiles be inquired of further, he will say that, although works go not before faith, they certainly come after.
positions.source: Ellicott's Bible Commentary for English Readers (text from the 1878 New Testament Commentary for English Readers, vol. 3) (scan errors corrected)

positions.text: Luther, supposing that James did actually teach the doctrine of justification by works, which his good sense showed him to be absolutely insufficient for salvation, was led to condemn the epistle in toto, as a production unauthenticated by the Holy Spirit, and consequently worthy of no regard; he therefore termed it epistola straminea, a chaffy epistle, an epistle of straw, fit only to be burnt.
positions.source: Adam Clarke, Commentary and Critical Notes (1810–26)
positions.ref: clarke (CrossWire SWORD module Clarke 2.0) on Jas 2:14

entries.question: Who the 144,000 are

positions.text: Some have thought that the sealed ones must be Jewish Christians; i.e., they are disposed to take the twelve tribes literally.
positions.source: Ellicott's Bible Commentary for English Readers (text checked against the 1878 New Testament Commentary for English Readers, vol. 3)

positions.text: The sealed ones are explained to be the servants of God; the description which follows proclaims them to be the “Israel of God.”
positions.source: Ellicott's Bible Commentary for English Readers (text checked against the 1878 New Testament Commentary for English Readers, vol. 3)

positions.text: the Israel of God
The early Christian church regarded itself symbolically as the Israel of God
The 144,000 probably represent all faithful Christians (cp. Rev 14:1-5; 21:12-17).

entries.question: Who or what the beast is, and the number 666

positions.text: The number 666 represents supernatural evil (see “Symbolic Numbers” Theme Note).
John might have used the transliteration Caesar Neron (a Hebrew spelling of the name) to arrive at the number 666.
A tradition emerged that the emperor Nero (AD 54–68) was so evil that he either did not really die or would be reincarnated as another tyrant like Domitian (AD 81–96).

The Praeterist in general maintains that the visions of the Apocalypse relate to events and circumstances which are past: the prophecies of the book—at least in their primary intention—have been fulfilled.
positions.source: Ellicott's Bible Commentary for English Readers (text checked against the 1878 New Testament Commentary for English Readers, vol. 3)

positions.text: The Futurist is at the opposite pole of interpretation, and maintains that the fulfilment of the book is still future, when our Lord will come again.
positions.source: Ellicott's Bible Commentary for English Readers (text checked against the 1878 New Testament Commentary for English Readers, vol. 3)

positions.text: Its advocates believe that in the Apocalypse we have a continuous prophecy, exhibiting to us the main features of the world's history: the visions therefore are partly fulfilled, partly they are in course of fulfilment, and a portion still remains unfulfilled.
positions.source: Ellicott's Bible Commentary for English Readers
positions.check: against a page scan before shipping (vol. 8 scan damaged; no second copy)

positions.text: The wild beast is always the figure of the kingdoms of this world—i.e., the kingdoms which are founded on passion or selfishness.
positions.source: Ellicott's Bible Commentary for English Readers (text checked against the 1878 New Testament Commentary for English Readers, vol. 3)

positions.text: The first of these alluded to finds the word in Nero Caesar. The second, and more ancient, finds it in Lateinos: this last was mentioned by Irenaeus.
positions.source: Ellicott's Bible Commentary for English Readers (text checked against the 1878 New Testament Commentary for English Readers, vol. 3) (scan errors corrected)

positions.text: It follows that the view here maintained does not exclude the possibility of a future personal Antichrist, in whom the typical features shall yet find clearer and fuller manifestation than in any previous age.
positions.source: Ellicott's Bible Commentary for English Readers
positions.check: against a page scan before shipping (vol. 8 scan damaged; no second copy)

positions.text: When Domitian became emperor (AD 81–96), he was as evil as Nero (both were fierce persecutors of the church), and many thought he was the embodiment of Nero's spirit, if not Nero himself (perhaps similar to the way that John the Baptist was considered to embody Elijah's spirit; see Mal 4:5; Matt 11:14; Luke 1:17; John 1:21).

entries.question: Whether the thousand years are literal, symbolic, or already under way

positions.text: Some scholars believe that this refers to a future period of time, while others believe that it refers to Jesus reigning now from heaven.

Premillennialism: The current age between Christ’s first and second comings will end when he returns to inaugurate a literal 1,000-year rule on earth with his holy people, after which Christ will execute the final judgment and inaugurate his eternal Kingdom.

Amillennialism: The “1,000 years” represents the current age between Christ’s first and second comings, in which Christ reigns spiritually with his people (i.e., there is not a literal 1,000-year period).

Postmillennialism: During the current age following Christ’s first coming, Christ will establish through the church an age of peace on earth (the 1,000 years), at the end of which Christ will return, execute the final judgment, and inaugurate his eternal Kingdom.

entries.question: What “this rock” is

positions.text: Some think that Peter is primarily important because of what he confessed about Jesus.
Others think that Peter and his successors have authority over the church.
Others think that Peter himself had authority over the early church but that he did not have any successors.
Some scholars have suggested that Jesus was referring to himself when he said this rock, but it seems clear that Jesus was referring either to Peter or to his confession.
Peter's confession is this rock as to doctrine.
positions.source: Matthew Henry, Concise Commentary on the Whole Bible
positions.ref: matthew-henry (CrossWire SWORD module MHCC 2.0) on Matt 16:13-20

entries.question: Whether eating the flesh and drinking the blood speaks of the Lord's Supper

positions.text: His words hinted at the Lord’s Supper yet to come (see Luke 22:19).
Since “flesh and blood” was a Jewish idiom for the whole person, Jesus might have been calling people to consume him fully by completely believing in him.
Some Christian traditions see the bread as Christ’s literal flesh broken for us and the wine as his literal blood poured out for us.
Others take the meaning in purely spiritual terms.

entries.question: Whether the longer ending was part of Mark
Whether the account of the woman caught in adultery was part of John
Whom “Your throne, O God” addresses: the king, God, or the Messiah

positions.text: The king is like a god among humans; he is anointed by God, he has received a mighty throne, and he dispenses justice as he rules forever.

One other possibility is that the psalmist could be addressing God directly but briefly in this sentence and then returning to address the king through the end of verse 9, after which he addresses the bride.

Because Hebrews 1:8–9 applies Psalm 45:6–7 to Christ, both Jewish and Christian traditions have often treated the psalm as Messianic, seeing the historical king and his bride as a type or foreshadowing of the ultimate King and his people.

entries.question: Who Gog is, and whether the battle is a literal event at the end of history

positions.text: Readers have long sought to identify Gog, who has sometimes been identified with Gyges, king of Lydia (about 680~644 BC).
Calmet says expressly, that Gog is Cambyses, king of Persia, who on his return from the land of Egypt, died in Judea.
positions.source: Adam Clarke, Commentary and Critical Notes (1810–26)
positions.ref: clarke (CrossWire SWORD module Clarke 2.0) on Ezek 38:2

positions.text: Gog, in the land of Magog, prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal, will invade the restored land of Israel from the far distant northern land by the appointment of God in the last times, and with a powerful army of numerous nations (ch. xxxviii. 1-9), with the intention of plundering Israel, now dwelling in security, that the Lord may sanctify Himself upon him before all the world (vers. 10-16).
positions.source: Keil and Delitzsch, Commentary on the Old Testament (1864–92) (scan errors corrected)
positions.side_suggested: a literal battle in the last times

entries.question: Whether the king of these verses is Antiochus IV or a figure beyond him

positions.text: Some interpreters see these verses as a transition from the earthly Antiochus IV to a character larger than history (7:8).
Most commentators believe these verses describe the time of the end of history (cp. Mark 13:14; 2 Thes 2:3-12; Rev 19:19-21).
Antiochus was a paradigm for future rulers who set themselves against the God of gods.
Antiochus IV thought himself equal to God (2 Maccabees 9:1–10:12), but God would hem him in until the time of wrath was completed.

entries.question: Whether Hosea's marriage to Gomer was real or an allegory, and what she was

positions.text: Many in the early church believed that the marriage did not actually take place.
Today, most interpreters regard the marriage as a real one, but they differ in their ideas about Gomer’s occupation prior to the marriage.
Some suggest that Gomer was an ordinary prostitute, while others suggest that she was one of the sacred prostitutes involved in Canaanite fertility worship.
Another possibility is that Gomer was a young woman who had not previously participated in illicit sexual activity, but whom God knew to be predisposed toward adultery and prostitution.

entries.question: Who “all Israel” is

positions.text: The phrase all Israel could refer to the total of all believers, both Jewish and Gentile; with this meaning, and so would describe the way that God works to bring salvation to all his people.

The restoration of the Jews is, in the course of things, far less improbable than the call of the Gentiles to be the children of Abraham; and though others now possess these privileges, it will not hinder their being admitted again.
positions.source: Matthew Henry, Concise Commentary on the Whole Bible
positions.ref: matthew-henry (CrossWire SWORD module MHCC 2.0) on Rom 11:22-32

positions.text: When this ingathering of the Gentiles is complete, then the turn of Israel will come round again, and the prophecies of their conversion will be fulfilled.
positions.source: Ellicott's Bible Commentary for English Readers (scan errors corrected)

entries.question: Whether the man is engaged to the virgin or is her father

positions.text: The apostle is thought to give advice here about the disposal of children in marriage.
positions.source: Matthew Henry, Concise Commentary on the Whole Bible
positions.ref: matthew-henry (CrossWire SWORD module MHCC 2.0) on 1 Cor 7:36-40

positions.text: The apostle by παρθενος, does not mean a virgin, but the state of virginity or celibacy, whether in man or woman.
positions.source: Adam Clarke, Commentary and Critical Notes (1810–26)
positions.ref: clarke (CrossWire SWORD module Clarke 2.0) on 1 Cor 7:36

entries.question: Whether “the women” are deacons' wives or women deacons

positions.text: These women, St. Chrysostom and most of the ancient expositors affirm, were deaconesses.
positions.source: Ellicott's Bible Commentary for English Readers
positions.held_by: St. Chrysostom and most of the ancient expositors

positions.text: I believe the apostle does not mean here the wives either of the bishops or deacons in particular, but the Christian women in general.
positions.source: Adam Clarke, Commentary and Critical Notes (1810–26)
positions.ref: clarke (CrossWire SWORD module Clarke 2.0) on 1 Tim 3:11

positions.text: In favor of their wives, 3:8-13 is a discussion of male deacons; switching to “women deacons” would disrupt the flow of thought.

entries.question: Who the spirits in prison are and what Christ proclaimed to them

positions.text: One interpretation holds that it refers to the spirits of people who have died and that Christ, after his resurrection, preached the Good News to these spirits.
A second interpretation sees 3:19-20 as describing Christ’s preaching through Noah to people who are now spirits in prison.
In the third interpretation, the spirits in prison are evil spiritual beings.

entries.question: Whether the gospel was preached to people after they died

positions.text: Some people believe that this clause means that Jesus went to hell and preached the gospel to people who had died before Jesus himself died on the cross.
Peter refers to people now dead who were exposed to the Good News while alive; he does not envision a chance to repent after death.
The gospel had been preached to those since dead, who by the proud and carnal judgment of wicked men were condemned as evil-doers, some even suffering death.
positions.source: Matthew Henry, Concise Commentary on the Whole Bible
positions.ref: matthew-henry (CrossWire SWORD module MHCC 2.0) on 1 Pet 4:1-6

entries.question: Who the two witnesses are

positions.text: Moses and Elijah, who appeared with Jesus at the transfiguration (Matt 17:3; Mark 9:4; Luke 9:30), are likely candidates (see Rev 11:6); they represent the law and the prophets.
Others have suggested Enoch and Elijah because they did not die (see Gen 5:21-24; 2 Kgs 2:11-12).
Other possibilities include Peter and Paul, or James and John.

The witnesses, then, stand as the typical representatives of those who, in the strength of God, have, through the long ages, borne witness for Christ against all wrong and falsehood, against a world in arms or a Church in error, or against a nominal Christianity in danger of becoming as corrupt and as cruel as heathenism.
positions.source: Ellicott's Bible Commentary for English Readers
